items.prompt: Project b = (1, 3, 2) onto the line through a = (2, 0, 1). The projection is t·a. What is t?
Your embeddings and query are all normalized to unit length. Does ranking by smallest Euclidean distance give the same order as ranking by largest cosine similarity?
options: No: distance and cosine measure different things
Yes: for unit vectors ‖e − q‖² = 2 − 2 cos θ, so the two orders match
Only in two dimensions
items.explain: ‖e − q‖² = ‖e‖² + ‖q‖² − 2e · q = 2 − 2 cos θ for unit vectors, which decreases as the cosine increases. Normalizing removes size, so only the angle is left for either measure.

items.prompt: A design matrix has an intercept, the outdoor temperature in °C, the same temperature in °F, and an indicator for each of 3 shifts (morning, afternoon, night). It has 6 columns. What is its rank?
items.explain: Two dependencies: °F = 32·(intercept) + 1.8·°C, and the three shift indicators add up to the intercept. 6 − 2 = 4.

items.prompt: You solve Ax = b with np.linalg.solve, where κ(A) ≈ 10¹⁴. The relative residual ‖Ax − b‖/‖b‖ is 10⁻¹⁶. How accurate is x?
options: Accurate to about 16 digits: the residual is tiny
It may have only about 2 correct digits: a tiny residual doesn't mean an accurate x when κ is large
Completely wrong: solve fails at this condition number
items.explain: solve is backward stable, so it exactly solves a problem within rounding of yours, which gives the tiny residual. With κ = 10¹⁴, that nearby problem's solution can differ from yours in all but the first couple of digits (16 − 14 = 2).

items.prompt: Which is the most accurate way to compute a least-squares fit when X is ill-conditioned?
options: np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y
np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
QR, or np.linalg.lstsq
items.explain: Both of the first two form XᵀX, whose condition number is κ(X)². QR and the SVD (which lstsq uses) work with κ(X) itself.

items.prompt: Fit y ≈ w·x through the origin (one coefficient) to x = (1, 2, 3) and y = (2, 3, 7). What is w?
items.explain: It's the projection of y onto the line through x: w = (x · y)/(x · x) = (2 + 6 + 21)/14 = 29/14 ≈ 2.07.

items.prompt: A discrete-time controller model has eigenvalues 0.5 ± 0.9i. Is it stable?
options: Yes: the real parts are below 1
No: |λ| = √(0.25 + 0.81) ≈ 1.03 > 1, so it oscillates with growing amplitude
It's neutrally stable
items.explain: Stability depends on the magnitude of each eigenvalue, not its real part. A complex pair rotates the state each step while scaling it by |λ| ≈ 1.03, so the oscillation grows by about 3% per step.

items.prompt: A two-node thermal model's matrix C⁻¹K has eigenvalues 0.02 and 0.5 per second. What is the slowest time constant, in seconds?
items.explain: Time constants are the reciprocals of the rates: 1/0.02 = 50 s and 1/0.5 = 2 s. The slowest mode is the one with the smallest eigenvalue.

items.prompt: Which of these symmetric matrices is positive definite?
items.explain: The eigenvalues are 1 and 3 for the first (positive definite), 4 and −2 for the second (indefinite: xᵀAx < 0 along (1, −1)) and 0 and 1 for the third (only semidefinite).

items.prompt: A matrix has singular values 5, 4, 1 and 0.5. What is the 2-norm error of its best rank-2 approximation?
items.explain: Eckart–Young: in the 2-norm, the error is the first singular value you drop, σ₃ = 1. (In the Frobenius norm it would be √(1² + 0.5²) ≈ 1.12.)

items.prompt: U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A). Which expression is the best rank-1 approximation of A?
options: s[0] * np.outer(U[:, 0], Vt[0])
s[0] * np.outer(U[0], Vt[:, 0])
items.explain: The first left singular vector is the first column of U and the first right singular vector is the first row of Vt; their outer product, scaled by σ₁, is σ₁u₁v₁ᵀ. The third option is a dot product, a single number.

items.prompt: You run PCA on 30 days of chiller-plant data: chilled-water temperatures (°C), pump powers (kW) and flows (L/s), without standardizing. The first component is almost entirely the flow columns. Why?
options: Flow matters most to the plant
The flow columns have the largest variance in their own units, so they dominate: standardize mixed-unit columns first
PCA always favours the last columns
items.explain: PCA ranks directions by variance, and variance depends on units: flows in L/s may vary by hundreds while temperatures vary by a few degrees. With mixed units, standardize (PCA on the correlation matrix).

items.prompt: Explain how least squares, orthogonal projection and the pseudoinverse fit together, and why you'd compute a fit with QR or the SVD rather than the normal equations.
rubric: The fitted vector Xw is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X, so the residual is perpendicular to every column (Xᵀ(y − Xw) = 0, the normal equations)
The pseudoinverse X⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ gives that solution, and the minimum-norm one when the columns are dependent
Forming XᵀX squares the condition number, so the normal equations lose twice as many digits
QR (Rw = Qᵀy) and the SVD work with X itself, keeping κ(X), and the SVD also reveals rank deficiency
items.explain: One picture (projection), one formula (pseudoinverse), and one numerical lesson (don't square κ).

delayedItems.prompt: Project b = (3, 0, 3) onto the line through a = (1, 2, 2). The projection is t·a. What is t?
Two sensors' hourly readings have a Pearson correlation of 0.98. What is the cosine similarity of their centered profiles?
options: 0.98: correlation is the cosine of centered vectors
It can't be determined without the means
delayedItems.explain: Pearson's correlation is exactly Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / (‖x − x̄‖‖y − ȳ‖), the cosine of the angle between the centered vectors.

delayedItems.prompt: A design matrix has an intercept, an indicator for each of the 4 seasons, the IT load in kW and the same load in W. It has 7 columns. What is its rank?
delayedItems.explain: Two dependencies: the season indicators add up to the intercept, and the W column is 1000 × the kW column. 7 − 2 = 5.

delayedItems.prompt: You build features T, T² and T³ from an outdoor temperature between 15 and 35 °C. What does standardizing T first do to the condition number of the feature matrix?
options: Nothing: rescaling never changes conditioning
It lowers it by orders of magnitude (about 2 × 10⁶ down to about 6 in this course's example)
It raises it, because standardized values are smaller
delayedItems.explain: Raw powers of a number near 25 point in nearly the same direction (all large and growing together), so the columns are nearly collinear. Centering and scaling first makes the powers far more distinct.

delayedItems.prompt: Why does solving least squares with QR avoid the normal equations' loss of accuracy?
options: It uses higher precision internally
It solves Rw = Qᵀy, and R has the same condition number as X instead of κ(X)²
It discards the smallest singular values
delayedItems.explain: Q is orthonormal, so multiplying by Qᵀ doesn't amplify errors, and κ(R) = κ(X). The normal equations work with XᵀX, whose condition number is κ(X)².

delayedItems.prompt: Fit y ≈ w·x through the origin (one coefficient) to x = (1, 1, 2) and y = (1, 3, 4). What is w?
A discrete-time model has eigenvalues 0.99 and −0.3. What does a disturbance do?
options: It grows
It decays, but slowly: after 100 steps the 0.99 mode is still at about 37% of its size
It oscillates forever at constant amplitude
delayedItems.explain: Both magnitudes are below 1, so it decays. The −0.3 mode flips sign and vanishes within a few steps; the 0.99 mode dominates, and 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.37.

delayedItems.prompt: A single thermal node has a heat capacity of 900 J/K and a 30 W/K conductance to the coolant. What is the largest stable forward-Euler time step, in seconds?
delayedItems.explain: The rate is λ = G/C = 1/30 per second (τ = 30 s), and forward Euler is stable for Δt ≤ 2/λ = 60 s.

delayedItems.prompt: A covariance matrix is estimated from 10 snapshots of 25 sensors. It is…
options: positive definite
positive semidefinite but singular, with rank at most 9
indefinite
delayedItems.explain: After centering, 10 snapshots span at most 9 directions, so at least 16 eigenvalues are zero. A covariance is always positive semidefinite; it's definite only with enough independent snapshots.

delayedItems.prompt: A matrix has singular values 5, 4, 1 and 0.5. What is the Frobenius-norm error of its best rank-2 approximation?
delayedItems.explain: Eckart–Young: √(σ₃² + σ₄²) = √(1 + 0.25) ≈ 1.118. In the 2-norm it would be σ₃ = 1.

delayedItems.prompt: A 3 × 3 matrix has singular values 3, 2 and 10⁻¹⁵. What is its numerical rank?
delayedItems.explain: 10⁻¹⁵ is below the usual tolerance (σ₁ × 3 × 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹⁵), so it counts as zero: rounding, not a real direction.

delayedItems.prompt: You fit POD modes on winter data and use them in summer to fill a dead sensor, when the economizer is off and the airflow pattern differs. What should you expect?
options: The same accuracy: modes describe the hall permanently
Possibly large errors, because the summer field may contain patterns the winter modes don't span; watch the residual on working sensors and refit
Better accuracy, because summer temperatures are higher
delayedItems.explain: Modes describe the data they were fitted on. A new operating mode can put energy in directions the old modes can't represent, which shows up as a growing reconstruction residual on the working sensors.

delayedItems.prompt: An agent wrote a PCA function for the inlet sensors. Explain how you would verify it before using it.
rubric: Checks the conventions: rows are snapshots, columns are centered (and scaled only if units differ), modes taken from Vt
Asserts invariants: orthonormal modes, reconstruction from all modes equals the data, energy fractions sum to 1
Compares with a trusted implementation (np.linalg.eigh of the covariance, or scikit-learn) up to sign
Tests on synthetic data with known modes, and evaluates anything learned on held-out snapshots
delayedItems.explain: Conventions, invariants, an independent reference and synthetic ground truth catch nearly every plausible-looking PCA bug.
